KIDS GAMES LESSON · KIDS GAMES · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bowling — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches hallway bowling — the rolling game where the counting after each roll is half the fun.

What is this?

Bowling is a rolling game: send the ball along the floor to knock over the pins standing at the other end.

What does it mean?

Rolling teaches the arm to push straight and low, and the counting between turns turns a game into a math lesson wearing bowling shoes.

What does the child need to know?

You need a soft ball and pins — real ones, or cups, or empty plastic bottles with a little rice inside so they stand up.

Why this matters

Rolling comes earlier than throwing for most children, and bowling gives the roll a job: the pins are waiting to be knocked, and they make a wonderful sound doing it.

What it teaches

Straight-line rolling, counting fallen pins, and the full game loop of knock-down, count and set-up-again.

Words to learn

bowlrollpinsknockcountset upagain

Say this to your child

“"Roll it low and slow — rrrroll! Look at the pins go down! How many fell? One, two, three! Now we set them up for the next bowler."”

Step by step

  1. Set the pins up in a triangle together — point them at the thrower.
  2. Stand back — three big steps is a fair first distance.
  3. Swing the ball between your legs or push it with both hands.
  4. Roll it LOW — a ball that flies is a ball that misses.
  5. Count the fallen pins out loud, then set them up for the next bowler.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the pink ball rolls up the lane toward ten white pins standing in their triangle — the triangle shape is how real pins stand, so every ball can knock more than one.

Ask your child

"How many pins fell?" "Which is louder — a strike or a gutter ball?" "Can you roll it slow enough that the last pin falls last?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might invent strike dances, roll one pin at a time on purpose to make the game last, or insist on setting the pins up alone — the engineer of the alley.

Out in the real world

Bowling alleys rent small balls and light pins for exactly this game — the hallway version is the try-out, and the real lanes are the graduation.

Try it together

Fair turns: one roll each, two rolls if you are feeling generous, and the set-up job travels with the turn. Three bottles is a hallway alley; ten is a championship.

Understanding check

Ask: "Does the ball roll high or low?" (low) "What do we do after we knock the pins?" (count them, then set them up)

This lesson pairs with the Bowling flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Kids Games.
